 Dengue deaths surpass 500, outbreak likely to persist into December 
 Three more people have died of dengue, taking this year’s death toll to 502, while 1,598 new patients were admitted to hospitals across the country in the 24 hours. 
 Tawsia Tajmim 
 16 November, 2026, 09:50 pm 
 Last modified: 17 November, 2026, 12:43 pm 
 Illustration: TBS "> 
 Illustration: TBS 
 The death toll from dengue in Bangladesh has crossed 500 this year, and experts fear the outbreak could continue into December as the situation has shown little improvement even in mid-November. 
 Infograph: TBS "> 
 Infograph: TBS 
 They say this year's dengue season is lasting longer than usual. The spread of infections in rural areas, coupled with inadequate mosquito-control measures instead of effective prevention, is making the situation more complicated. 
 Dr Khabirul Bashar, medical entomologist and professor of zoology at Jahangirnagar University, told The Business Standard that dengue would remain widespread throughout November, with little likelihood of significant improvement in December. 
 "Compared with previous years, the number of dengue patients could be higher this December," he said. 
 Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel
 He said the transmission cycle of dengue had not been broken. Rainfall in November has created fresh favourable conditions for Aedes mosquitoes to breed, raising the risk of continued transmission into December. 
 Experts say August, September and October are generally the peak months for dengue in Bangladesh, although infections sometimes remain high in November. This year, the outbreak has continued at a significant level into the month. 
 They also believe the traditional dengue season in Bangladesh is changing. In previous years, infections would generally begin to decline after the monsoon, particularly in November and December. But with transmission expected to continue into December this year, the risk may persist even during winter. 
 Three more people have died of dengue, taking this year's death toll to 502, while 1,598 new patients were admitted to hospitals across the country in the 24 hours until 8am today (16 November), according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). 
 The DGHS said dengue claimed 83 lives in the first 16 days of November, compared with 174 in October, 148 in September, 43 in August, 36 in July and 13 in June. 
 Hospital admissions reached around 29,880 in November so far, following 53,000 in October, 43,774 in September, 20,536 in August, 9,206 in July and 2,907 in June. 
 The cumulative number of dengue cases reported nationwide has reached 1,64,107 this year. 
 Dr Benazir Ahmed, public health expert and former director of the disease control division at the DGHS, told TBS that two major factors were behind the high number of infections and deaths this year. 
 "First, changes in rainfall patterns since June and frequent rainfall have created more favourable breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. Second, dengue is no longer confined to Dhaka and other major cities; transmission has become established in rural areas as well," he said. 
 Benazir said dengue patients were being identified in rural areas of different districts, including Bogura and Bhola. When someone in a village develops a severe infection, access to advanced medical treatment is relatively limited. Delays in reaching hospitals in major cities can leave patients in more critical condition. 
 Dr Benazir warned that the spread of dengue in rural areas could develop into a long-term public health crisis. Areas where transmission has become established will remain vulnerable to repeated outbreaks, potentially making dengue control an even greater challenge for Bangladesh in the coming years. 
 Larval control remains neglected 
 Experts say one of the biggest shortcomings in the government's dengue-control efforts is the failure to adequately destroy Aedes mosquito breeding sites. Simply clearing bushes, removing dust or conducting fogging operations cannot bring dengue under control. 
 Dr Benazir said an Integrated Vector Management (IVM) approach was needed to control Aedes mosquitoes. Its two main components are removing artificial containers and other objects where water accumulates, and applying larvicides in places where stagnant water cannot be drained. 
 "Excessive reliance on fogging was not an effective dengue-control strategy. Fogging mainly targets adult mosquitoes and may be used on a limited scale when the density of adult Aedes mosquitoes becomes high in a particular area," he said. 
 However, removing stagnant water and applying larvicides must receive the highest priority to prevent mosquitoes from breeding, he added. 
 According to him, mosquito-control infrastructure and manpower outside Dhaka remain weak. While mosquito-control programmes have been conducted in the capital for years, the capacity to carry out similar activities in districts and rural areas is much more limited. This is making it increasingly difficult to prevent dengue from spreading in villages. 
 Professor Khabirul Bashar also stressed the importance of managing breeding sites, applying larvicides and increasing community participation in dengue prevention. 
 Isolated drives cannot stop the spread of Aedes mosquitoes, he said, emphasising the need for regular and coordinated control efforts.
